candidates.text:
It is 1976. Ingvar Kamprad has moved his family to Denmark, further from Älmhult. IKEA is opening new stores constantly, and the everyday talks with his co-workers are mostly gone. So he writes the culture down in nine points and calls it The Testament of a Furniture Dealer.

I thought about it a lot last week, when Quartr held its first ever company-wide summit. 150+ people from New York, Dublin, Stockholm and Gothenburg, in the same room for the first time.

I joined almost five years ago, part time, while I was still at university. I found the company through people on this app, and my first job had nothing to do with design. Today I have been given responsibility for our brand team. That says less about me than about the people who trusted me with it.

People who knew Kamprad say he loved meeting the staff in his stores, and would often hug them and thank them. I understand that better now. Most of my colleagues were a name and a green dot on Slack. Some I had worked with for years. Last week we shook hands for the first time. I had goosebumps.

Kamprad wrote that anyone with leadership responsibility must "motivate and develop your co-workers." Charlie Munger said the best culture is "a seamless web of deserved trust." Hire good people and trust them to do what they do best. We give that trust early, and everyone earns it every day.

We come from many different countries and bring different ideas about business and life. "We must look after each other and inspire each other," the testament says. In Stockholm, I watched us do both.

Kamprad wrote that any designer can draw a desk for 5,000 kronor, and only the most skilled can make a good one for 100. We're a small Swedish company, never the best-funded in our space. Small means are not our excuse. They are our method. The test is to keep building the 100-kronor desk once we can afford the other one. IKEA still hands the testament to every new employee, long after it stopped being small.

Kamprad wrote it down because he could no longer be in the room. This time, we were.

The last chapter of the testament is called "Most things still remain to be done." It was true in Älmhult in 1976. It was true in Stockholm last week.

To everyone in that room, thank you. And if you want to be part of it, reach out to me.

candidates.text:
Adam Neumann on why top-down management fails with great talent:

"Top to bottom means you think because someone reports in to you, they have to do what you say."

"But it's not true. This is not a dictatorship. They have free will."

"If you hired someone, they're really talented, they'll go work elsewhere. The more talented they are, the more the top to bottom does not work. They won't be willing to do it. They shouldn't."

"Great talent is not willing to be managed like this."

"If you're gonna manage these employees and you wanna attract the best talent in the world, remember that power comes from influence, not control."

"If you think they need to do what you said because you're their boss, you've already lost, and it's a matter of time till it doesn't work out. If they're okay with it... they're not the right employee for you, and you're not the right boss for them. There's no chance you're getting the best out of them."

@AdamNeumann w/ @StevenBartlett

SF Compute CEO @evanjconrad says if there's an AI bubble, VCs funding AI labs at massive valuations are the ones holding the risk.

"If you're looking for a bubble, it's held currently by the venture capitalists."

"The AI bubble works like this: the cloud itself doesn't deploy the GPU cluster until they have the contract in hand from the customer."

"Then they force the customer to pay them a massive deposit upfront so that they can give it to the OEM, who then gives it off to Nvidia."

"But the AI lab itself doesn't have that capital yet because they need it for the future. So they go off and they raise money at massive valuations."

"And all the VCs look around and say, 'Well, I guess we missed out on OpenAI and Anthropic. Maybe these people will be OpenAI and Anthropic too. We'll go with the big valuation.'"

"But then the venture capitalist owns the risk."

our company policy is simple: write “human written” at the top if it’s not written by ai. we expect 98% of stuff to be written by ai.

but more importantly we do not produce unnecessary docs. we just share basic artifacts to get things done that are more than likely generated by ai. our slack has context that is accessible by ai for any sort of truth keeping & it’s all very easy to query through @ claude for example.

the broader reality is that ai will be used as an intermediary to read & write. why fight it? these policies aren’t even necessary for the most part because every current thing will be outdated in few months anyway. i.e. how we collaborate or work etc is constantly being reshaped at lightening speeds.

The best emerging VCs are highly technical, according to Plexo Capital MP @Lo_Toney:

“The thing that I really have noticed is that the GPs that are just getting started in their career — the best GPs are much more technical. Even within the last 10 years, I think that’s the biggest evolution that I’ve seen.”

“When you look at the GPs that we see today with the smaller funds, these are folks that are coming in with a very unique perspective. And the edge, I think, translates directly from their technical understanding of a problem they had to tackle within one of these technology companies.”

“What that does is it opens their eyes to this really unique set of problems that they know can’t be solved, but they understand the technical limitations of the current solutions as to why those problems can’t be solved.”

“They kind of have somewhat of an idea about the perspective of, ‘Hey, this is how I think this problem could be solved. But maybe there’s one aspect that’s missing. Maybe it’s the compute horsepower, or maybe there’s a certain problem that hasn’t been solved on an architecture side. There’s something that’s just missing.’”

“They know what to look for, and then when they see it, they can pounce on it immediately.”
